name: Fruit juice cleanse

lead: A juice cleanse means drinking only fruit and vegetable juice for a few days, usually to detox or reset. It is popular online and among celebrities.
Health bodies such as the American Cancer Society and Harvard Health state there is no scientific evidence for the claimed benefits.

paras: Believers say it clears toxins; dietitians say the liver and kidneys already do that work. Weight lost is mostly regained afterwards according to reviews.
Possible dizziness, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes; long unsupervised fasts can cause deficiencies.

lead: A fruit juice cleanse, also called juice fasting or juice cleansing, is a short-term diet, usually one to seven days, in which a person drinks only fruit and vegetable juices and eats no solid food [1]. It is promoted as a way to detoxify the body and is treated as a form of detox diet [1][2].

Proponents say periodic cleanses remove unwanted chemicals [1]. Organisations including the American Cancer Society and Harvard Health state that there is no scientific evidence supporting juice-only diets for such benefits [1].

paras: Norman W. Walker designed an early mechanical juicer in 1936, and his books on raw, mostly liquid diets helped shape the modern cleanse. Jay Kordich popularised juicing in the 1990s through a bestselling book and infomercials. Celebrities and online users have kept juice diets in circulation since [1].

Catherine Collins, a hospital dietitian, has called detox a marketing concept rather than a physiological process [1]. Harvard Health has stated that no published research supports the safety or effectiveness of juice cleanses [1]. Even advocate Joe Cross has described his plan as a short reboot rather than a long-term solution [1].

A 2015 review of detox diets generally found no compelling evidence for toxin removal or weight management, and a 2017 review reported that short-term weight loss from calorie restriction is regained [2].

Reference works list possible metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes or hypoglycaemia, dizziness from falling blood pressure, diarrhoea leading to dehydration, and protein or calcium deficiency in long unsupervised fasts [1]. A 2018 case report linked a green-smoothie cleanse to oxalate kidney injury [2].
No studies found on juice cleanses for appearance outcomes.
